data.title: 3 Funds With Capital Market Exposure After Anthropic’s Record IPO
data.description:
Two funds both tied to capital markets can look similar on paper, yet one like IAI can be almost 100% in investment banks and exchanges, while another like IYF has less than a third there and far more in broader financials. That split matters when a company like Anthropic lists in a record US$81.3b IPO and pushes large underwriting and trading volumes through the system. Those flows feed directly into the businesses that run the deals and platforms. Investors looking to explore that angle can consider how IAI, KCE and IYF provide three distinct ETF approaches to this area of the market.

iShares U.S. Broker-Dealers & Securities Exchanges ETF (IAI)

Holdings: 40 | In capital markets: 99.8% of the fund

Goldman Sachs at 17.76% is a large Wall Street investment bank that helps run IPO books, so a jumbo deal like the Anthropic listing can mean more advisory and underwriting revenue flowing through a major slice of IAI. Morgan Stanley at 15.07% also leans on capital markets work, while Charles Schwab at 8.55% is closer to retail brokerage and trading volumes. Together, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley make up 32.8% of this ETF. This gives you a concentrated tilt toward investment banking and brokerage, alongside exchanges and data groups that sit on 40.2% of the portfolio by industry weight.

You are effectively betting that investment banks and trading platforms keep finding enough deal flow and turnover to justify such a focused approach, with 99.8% of the fund in capital markets businesses. Simply Wall St's fair value work suggests 56.1% of IAI by weight is in holdings trading below its estimates of fair value. Some investors may see this as a reason to research this ETF further. Heavy reliance on a handful of big brokers and dealers is the flip side, because any sector wide slump in underwriting or trading activity would hit a large portion of your exposure at once.

State Street SPDR S&P Capital Markets ETF (KCE)

This ETF gives you a broad mix of capital markets businesses that can all touch an Anthropic sized IPO in different ways. Asset managers and custody banks make up 45.4% of the portfolio, with another 29.0% in investment banking and brokerage and 25.4% in exchanges and data. Donnelley Financial Solutions and Tradeweb Markets together are 4.3% of the fund, while Cboe Global Markets adds listed trading infrastructure that can see more activity when a high profile new listing starts trading. About 34% of KCE overlaps with IAI, so much of the rest is in capital markets companies IAI does not hold.

The ETF relies on the S&P Capital Markets Select Industry Index to keep the focus on capital markets, and on a spread of 68 holdings where Simply Wall St estimates that 45.2% of the fund by weight sits below its fair value estimates. iShares U.S. Financials ETF (IYF)

This ETF gives you a capital markets link through Berkshire Hathaway at 13.04% and JPMorgan Chase at 10.93%, which together are a heavy 24.0% of the fund. Both can benefit if an Anthropic scale IPO feeds more underwriting revenue, trading activity and related banking work into their broader franchises. Underwriters and trading platforms need to keep a strong grip on allocations and aftermarket activity for this to matter.

data.title: We Think You Can Look Beyond Trade Desk's (NASDAQ:TTD) Lackluster Earnings
data.description:
The Trade Desk, Inc.'s (NASDAQ:TTD) stock was strong despite it releasing a soft earnings report last week. We think that investors might be looking at some positive factors beyond the earnings numbers.

This technology could replace computers: discover the 20 stocks are working to make quantum computing a reality.

Examining Cashflow Against Trade Desk's Earnings

Many investors haven't heard of the accrual ratio from cashflow, but it is actually a useful measure of how well a company's profit is backed up by free cash flow (FCF) during a given period. In plain english, this ratio subtracts FCF from net profit, and divides that number by the company's average operating assets over that period. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

Therefore, it's actually considered a good thing when a company has a negative accrual ratio, but a bad thing if its accrual ratio is positive. While it's not a problem to have a positive accrual ratio, indicating a certain level of non-cash profits, a high accrual ratio is arguably a bad thing, because it indicates paper profits are not matched by cash flow. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

For the year to September 2026, Trade Desk had an accrual ratio of -0.47. That indicates that its free cash flow quite significantly exceeded its statutory profit. To wit, it produced free cash flow of US$847m during the period, dwarfing its reported profit of US$329.4m. Trade Desk shareholders are no doubt pleased that free cash flow improved over the last twelve months.

Based on this observation, we consider it possible that Trade Desk's statutory profit actually understates its earnings potential! And on top of that, its earnings per share have grown at an extremely impressive rate over the last three years. data.title: There May Be Some Bright Spots In Humana's (NYSE:HUM) Earnings

AI is about to change healthcare. These 20 stocks are working on everything from early diagnostics to drug discovery. The best part - they are all under $10bn in marketcap - there is still time to get in early.

Zooming In On Humana's Earnings

Many investors haven't heard of the accrual ratio from cashflow, but it is actually a useful measure of how well a company's profit is backed up by free cash flow (FCF) during a given period. To get the accrual ratio we first subtract FCF from profit for a period, and then divide that number by the average operating assets for the period. The ratio shows us how much a company's profit exceeds its FCF.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. While having an accrual ratio above zero is of little concern, we do think it's worth noting when a company has a relatively high accrual ratio. To quote a 2014 paper by Lewellen and Resutek, "firms with higher accruals tend to be less profitable in the future".

Over the twelve months to September 2026, Humana recorded an accrual ratio of -0.23. Therefore, its statutory earnings were very significantly less than its free cashflow. To wit, it produced free cash flow of US$3.1b during the period, dwarfing its reported profit of US$1.25b. Humana shareholders are no doubt pleased that free cash flow improved over the last twelve months. Having said that, there is more to the story. We can see that unusual items have impacted its statutory profit, and therefore the accrual ratio.

How Do Unusual Items Influence Profit?

Humana's profit was reduced by unusual items worth US$432m in the last twelve months, and this helped it produce high cash conversion, as reflected by its unusual items. In a scenario where those unusual items included non-cash charges, we'd expect to see a strong accrual ratio, which is exactly what has happened in this case. It's never great to see unusual items costing the company profits, but on the upside, things might improve sooner rather than later. We looked at thousands of listed companies and found that unusual items are very often one-off in nature. And that's hardly a surprise given these line items are considered unusual. Assuming those unusual expenses don't come up again, we'd therefore expect Humana to produce a higher profit next year, all else being equal.

Our Take On Humana's Profit Performance

Considering both Humana's accrual ratio and its unusual items, we think its statutory earnings are unlikely to exaggerate the company's underlying earnings power. data.title: Here's What We Like About Jefferson Capital's (NASDAQ:JCAP) Upcoming Dividend
data.description:
Jefferson Capital, Inc. (NASDAQ:JCAP) is about to trade ex-dividend in the next 4 days. The ex-dividend date occurs one day before the record date, which is the day on which shareholders need to be on the company's books in order to receive a dividend. The ex-dividend date is important because any transaction on a stock needs to have been settled before the record date in order to be eligible for a dividend. Thus, you can purchase Jefferson Capital's shares before the 24th of November in order to receive the dividend, which the company will pay on the 3rd of December.

The company's next dividend payment will be US$0.24 per share, on the back of last year when the company paid a total of US$0.96 to shareholders. Based on the last year's worth of payments, Jefferson Capital stock has a trailing yield of around 4.5% on the current share price of US$21.12. Dividends are a major contributor to investment returns for long term holders, but only if the dividend continues to be paid. So we need to investigate whether Jefferson Capital can afford its dividend, and if the dividend could grow.

Dividends are usually paid out of company profits, so if a company pays out more than it earned then its dividend is usually at greater risk of being cut. Fortunately Jefferson Capital's payout ratio is modest, at just 37% of profit.

When a company paid out less in dividends than it earned in profit, this generally suggests its dividend is affordable. The lower the % of its profit that it pays out, the greater the margin of safety for the dividend if the business enters a downturn.

Given that Jefferson Capital has only been paying a dividend for a year, there's not much of a past history to draw insight from.

This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. While having an accrual ratio above zero is of little concern, we do think it's worth noting when a company has a relatively high accrual ratio. To quote a 2014 paper by Lewellen and Resutek, "firms with higher accruals tend to be less profitable in the future".

Crown Crafts has an accrual ratio of -0.18 for the year to September 2026. That implies it has very good cash conversion, and that its earnings in the last year actually significantly understate its free cash flow. To wit, it produced free cash flow of US$14m during the period, dwarfing its reported profit of US$5.17m. Crown Crafts' free cash flow improved over the last year, which is generally good to see.

The key marker is whether Rio Tinto Group hits its October to December 2027 timetable for restarting and fully ramping Line 4 at Tiwai Point while visibly progressing Panguna remediation projects. On time delivery for both would support the idea that the group can balance environmental repair spending with operational expansion using renewables.

data.title: Newmont Stock Has The Bull Case Changed After The Metals Sell Off?
data.description:
• Newmont filed an August 2026 construction update with US regulators on repairs at its Blue Lake penstock, while higher expected all in sustaining costs and rising 2027 development spending underline ongoing capital and inflation pressures on the mining portfolio.
  • A sharp sell-off in precious and industrial metals, linked to rate hike expectations and weaker copper sentiment, hit Newmont just as investors were reassessing its long life gold plus copper assets and cost reset efforts.
  • We will now look at how this metals sell off and higher projected unit costs could reshape Newmont’s longer term investment narrative.

Scan beyond Newmont to see how other gold producers are positioned after this metals sell off by reviewing the hand picked 33 elite gold producer stocks now shaping the sector reaction.

Newmont Investment Narrative Recap

To stay comfortable as a Newmont shareholder, you need to believe the business can manage higher all in sustaining costs while keeping its long life gold and copper portfolio productive. The current metals sell off and cost guidance reset put near term focus on cash generation and discipline rather than pure volume growth.

The key short term catalyst is how Newmont executes through rising 2027 development spending and inflation without eroding margins too sharply. The biggest risk sits in capital intensity, from Red Chris to projects like Lihir, where any delays, safety issues or further cost creep would pressure free cash flow and investor confidence.

The most relevant fresh datapoint is the August 2026 Blue Lake Penstock Repair Project construction report filed with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. It may look like a small hydro related footnote, yet it reinforces that Newmont is working through a series of infrastructure and legacy assets that all feed into operating reliability and regulatory relationships.

For you as an investor, that filing sits alongside the cost outlook and the metals pullback as part of the same story. Execution on projects like Blue Lake and Red Chris, together with the higher capex and inflation risks highlighted in the analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St, will shape whether Newmont turns its large project pipeline into stable production rather than recurring interruptions.

Newmont’s Analyst Assumptions in Context

Newmont's analyst narrative points to forecast revenue of US$31.4b and projected earnings of US$11.9b by 2029, built on expectations of 5.7% yearly revenue growth and an earnings increase of about US$2.7b from current earnings of US$9.2b.

Those headline figures sit on top of some bold assumptions. Analysts are effectively baking in both higher profit margins and a larger top line, with expectations that margins move from 34.7% today to 37.8% in three years. For you as a shareholder, that combination matters more than any single production target because it speaks directly to how much of every future gold and copper dollar might actually reach the bottom line.

The earnings ramp also comes with a wide spread of opinions. Forecasts cluster around US$11.9b in profit by 2029, but the range runs from US$9.5b to US$14.3b. That disagreement indicates that the path from today’s operations, through projects like Red Chris and the cost reset, to those future numbers is anything but straightforward.

In addition, the analyst framework assumes Newmont shrinks its share count by about 4.77% per year for the next three years. If that happens, per share figures would benefit even if absolute earnings only track the mid range of forecasts. If buybacks slow or pause because of higher capex or weaker metals pricing, that per share uplift would look very different.

Valuation work in these reports ties the 2029 earnings line to a P/E of 13.2x, slightly below the current multiple of 13.6x and also below the cited 15.5x for the wider US metals and mining industry. In this framework, analysts appear comfortable with Newmont earning a modest discount to peers while still ramping profit over time.

The consensus target price of US$135.47, compared with a current share price of US$120.91 as of November 2026, reflects how much weight the market is placing on those assumptions today. Some forecasters stretch to US$165.00, while the most cautious come in at US$70.00, which underlines how sensitive this story is to execution on costs, capital projects and movements in metals prices.

For anyone tracking Newmont after the recent metals sell off, these metrics provide a clear checklist. Revenue growing near 5.7% a year, earnings stepping from US$9.2b to a potential US$11.9b, margins edging higher and the share count declining all need to align for the analyst case to hold together.

Exploring Other Perspectives

One optimistic twist in the alternate Newmont story is the capital returns angle. The most bullish analysts were modelling about US$40.2b of 2029 revenue and US$14.8b of earnings, helped by ongoing buybacks and record free cash flow. After the Blue Lake update and metals sell off, you can expect some of those assumptions to be revisited, so treat them as one of several viewpoints to stress test rather than as a blueprint.
